utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, call your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. Waespi will be handling the first witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just so Your Honours know, I will be sitting in only for the first session and then another lawyer for our team will be in the for the remainder of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're blessed with an abundance of riches.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I certainly am. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. The first Prosecution witness will be Mr. David Harland. And perhaps, Mr. President, while we are waiting, in your decision of the 12th January of this year, you have accepted our motion to have selected parts of his prior testimony admitted under Rule 92 ter, and as you are aware, the witness testified in the Slobodan Milosevic case on two days, the 18th September, 2003, mainly examination-in-chief and a little bit of cross-examination; and on the 5th of November, 2003, he was re-called for the end of cross-examination, a few questions by the amici and re-direct examination. So once the witness is in, Mr. President, Your Honours, I will ask that he, you know, certify, according to the Rules, that these two testimonies can be formally tendered. And perhaps since I'm new to e-court, I'm not entirely sure whether I actually give him a hard copy of his two transcripts in the Milosevic case and have him confirm that this is in the transcript or whether he actually looks at the transcript on the screen. There have been 65 ter numbers assigned to these transcripts so it could be done electronically, but I'm in your hands as how it is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, since we are beginning it might be well that you provide him with hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I hope you have well rested?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Very well-rested, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state for the record were full name.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: David John Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we did meet yesterday in my office, and I showed you the record of your testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic case. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the court usher please could hand over to Mr. Harland a hard copy of those two transcripts, I would be mush obliged. Please show it to the Defence first so that they can see that it's an authentic record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harland, before coming to testify today, did you have a chance to review your testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And are you satisfied and can you attest today to the Court that these transcripts accurately reflect your evidence in that case and the answers you would give now, today, if asked about the same matters under oath would be the same?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 65 ter numbers assigned, and that was done over e-mail, just for the record I'll just say what we have been told was that the transcript of the 18th September, 2003, have been assigned ter number 02815. And the second testimony, that's 5th November, 2003, the ter number assigned is 02816. And I propose, Your Honours, that at the end of his testimony, perhaps at the end of cross-examination and questions by Your Honours, we'll move or we will move to have all these exhibits admitted in one go, rather than step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harland, can you tell us your profession, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I'm a civil servant with the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what's your current function?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I'm the director for Europe and Latin America of the Department of Peacekeeping Operations at United Nations headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's in New York?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That's in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks. Could you briefly give for the benefit of Your Honours and Defence the background of your career, your education, your career in the UN very briefly, because it's an impressive career?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I did my undergraduate studies in my home country, New Zealand. I then pursued graduate studies in law and in international relations, and took a master's degree from Harvard University in the United States, a study in comparative law, and a Ph.D. from the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy. I served with the United Nations extensively for almost 20 years in Africa, in Europe, and in Asia and in -- principally in conflict and post-conflict countries. And now, for almost four years, I've been based in New York, my first assignment at UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland. Now, of course we know from your Slobodan Milosevic testimony that you were in Bosnia and in Sarajevo. Now, for how long were you in Sarajevo and when exactly, what was that period?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I was a civil affairs officer with UNPROFOR initially, and I arrived in the first half of 1993, and I was based in Sarajevo and Kiseljak. I remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the war as head of civil affairs of the United Nations mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then I stayed on for almost one additional year in 1999, preparing the report of United Nations Secretary-General on the massacre at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what were the duties of a civil affairs officer? What were your duties while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: My principal duties were to make political assessments of the progress of the conflict in that country and to -- in order to do that, to meet regularly with members of the warring factions and also to attempt to negotiate with them measures to mitigate the -- the conflict by securing freedom of movement for civilians or the restoration of essential services to civilians or agreements between the parties that could limit the -- the effect of the war on the civilian population of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that part of your duties was to draft reports?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I did a lot of drafting. I was the principal political drafter for UNPROFOR and Sarajevo for the whole period of the war that I was there. I drafted all of the special reports, all of the weekly political assessments of UNPROFOR headquarters. I also drafted the text of most of the agreements between the warring factions, which were done under the auspices of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe in the Slobodan Milosevic case you were introduced as the longest-serving UN official in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I believe that is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I just have one last kind of general questions before we go into details. Can you tell the Judges, very briefly if you can, your memory of Sarajevo, and as you know this case is concerned with the events after the signing of the anti-sniping agreement in August 1994. So when you think about Sarajevo, about the atmosphere at that time, what can you tell to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, I -- I arrived in Sarajevo in the first half of 1993 when the siege had been closed for almost a year. The streets were entirely empty except for some burnt-out vehicles. There was nobody, basically, on the -- on the street. There was the constant background noise of either small-arms fire from the -- the front lines around the city or from the -- the heavy weapons, detonations from the Serbian bombardment. It -- it was, in a sense, eerily empty. People would come out for very, very short periods to collect water from water-dispensing points or a little bit of food and then they would scurry back into their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the way I would like to conduct this examination-in-chief is the following: First, I would like him to clarify four transcript references from the Slobodan Milosevic case; and then I will ask him a few questions about -- I think it's about 20 documents, some of them Mr. Harland drafted himself and others he has seen or he knows something about the authenticity of these documents. So that's the basic outline. I think we might be finished within the first session or it might spill a little bit over the next session. So with your leave, Mr. President, I would like to ask him a couple of points in clarification of his Milosevic testimony. The first reference, Mr. President, Your Honours, can be found in his first day of testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic case, again that's the 18th September, 2003, and it's on page 26935. And I read it for the record, Your Honours, and for everybody's benefit. It's on line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Harland, in this part you talk about a meeting you had in mid-July 1993 with Bosnian Serb leaders, and you make the following comment, and I quote you from your Slobodan Milosevic testimony: "Yes, Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders emphasised to us that their principal goal was to force the Bosnian government to -- to negotiate peace, a peace agreement on terms that would be acceptable to them and that the reason they were shelling Sarajevo, for example, which I think was what we were protesting about that day was to apply pressure on the Bosnian government." Now, what you testified about in mid-July 1993, did the same mechanism also apply after the period of August 1994, or was that exclusively confined to the 1993 situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No. It applied to the whole period of the -- of the war. The basic dynamic of the conflict around Sarajevo was that the Serbs, who were in a completely militarily dominant position, would use shelling and sniping against civilians as a way to elicit from the Bosnian government behaviour they wanted, and we knew this was their essential purpose for two reasons. First, they told us so. The transcript which you referred to is just one example of how they explained to us that they wanted to apply pressure, as they called it, to the Bosnian government by waging this war of terror against the civilian population. And also we knew it because it -- from observing their behaviour. Most of the -- most of the military activity that I was reporting on was not military activity as we would conventionally understand it. Most of it was undirected or semi-directed artillery fire against civilian-inhabited areas. And one could very easily detect patterns of an increase of such application of terror, you know, whether through bombardment from heavy weapons or snipers or through cutting off electricity and water and food at times of -- when they wanted to achieve greater political leverage. For example, during the Owen-Stoltenberg peace process when the Bosnian government appeared to be stalling on elements of the peace package which were acceptable to the Serbs, there would be a significant increase in these -- this war of terror. The increase of the privations by cutting off the city and an increase in the sniping against civilians and the bombardment -- the random bombardment of the city. And that dynamic continued right through until the end of the war in October 1995. And my own assumption at the time - and I don't think anybody really disagreed with it - was that indeed the principal activity of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was the -- the application of these instruments of terror against the civilian population; that was what they basically did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland. Let me turn to the second quote from your Slobodan Milosevic testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that's on page 26936, beginning at line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And your answer, Mr. Harland, is the following: "Well, most obviously, of course, it's another example of the Serb modulating their military effort and modulating the amount of terror; that is, the amount of humanitarian difficulty placed on the population of Sarajevo to, in the context of a -- for political objectives; that is, of getting the Muslims to negotiate or in terms of deterring any NATO military attack on them. Our sense was they -- there was, as it were, a spigot of terror which they would open or close according to how much pressure was on them from the international community or what political concessions they hoped to get from the other side." And I believe you almost answered this question as well with your previous answer. Would that quote, which is specifically directed at the 1993 situation in the Slobodan Milosevic case, would that also apply to the period after the signature of the anti-sniping agreement in August 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And it -- obviously, the level of terror, the extent to which the spigot was more open or more closed varied a lot between 1993 and 1995, but the basic dynamic was the same. They attempted to inflict maximum suffering on the people of Sarajevo to induce the Bosnian government authorities to accept a peace agreement on terms agreeable to the Serbs, but they never applied what they believed was too much pressure, that it would lead to the withdrawal of UNPROFOR or to a wider western military intervention. And they were always relatively sensitive to that -- and, in fact, this basic dynamic which is being discussed in the quotation you refer to was the dominant military pattern. There was little conventional force-on-force military activity. The principal application of force was not, as would be understood by any modern military logic, it was purely for these objectives of the application of terror against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, the next quote, the third one from the Slobodan Milosevic case, can be found on the next page in your transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, Your Honours, it's on page 26937.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: There you discuss the comparative military activity in the years 1993, 1994, and 1995, and I quote: "1993 was the most militarily active of those years. There was a conflict, both between the Bosnian government, that is, that Muslims and the Serbs; and between the Bosnian government and the Croats. 1994 was relatively quiet throughout most of the year, and then 1995 saw a sharp deterioration again right up to the end of the war in October." That was from line 15 to line 20. If you can, Mr. Harland, elaborate a little bit on the sharp deterioration you mentioned here in 1995. We might see a couple of documents later, but can you tell Their Honours what's meant by the sharp deterioration in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I should first preface it by saying that this answer is correct with respect to the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina; but with respect to Sarajevo, I would say that 1995 was the most militarily active of the -- of the three years being discussed here. Now, in terms of the -- the sharp deterioration in 1995, I would actually say that this deterioration began towards the end of 1994. 1994 had been a relatively stable year. The Serbs had already taken almost all -- more than the land they ultimately sought to keep under the peace agreement. They would discuss this openly with us. Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik would regularly discuss what they thought were the final holdings they thought they would take. And they had on the ground I think a little over 70 percent of the total territory of the country. And they anticipated that they would have to give some of that territory back in the context of a peace agreement. And they described their military tactics to us as to hold on to the greater amount of land they had and then to let the Muslims, as they referred to the Bosnian government, to let the Muslims understand that they had no military options and that the suffering of their people would only greatly increase if the Bosnian government did not agree to a political settlement with the Serbs that would lead to Serb independence within defined borders, no reversal of ethnic cleansing, and a substantial acceptance of the territory they held. And 1992 and 1993 were largely devoted by the Serbs to gaining that territory and then removing the non-Serb population from those territories. During 1994, they were largely content to sit back and wait, hold on to the territory they had, apply what they called the pressure on the Muslim population, and -- and then to wait for a peace agreement acceptable to them. And they were -- they were very open with us. They thought that time was on their side. They said, you know, we hold all the land, we dominate all the high ground, we can apply pressure - as they called it - the shelling and the sniping and the cutting off of the water and gas and electricity and food to the Muslim population. And they thought all they had to do was wait and that in good time the Muslims would accept an agreement, roughly like the Owen-Stoltenberg Agreement, where the Muslims would be left with a small wedge of territory on which they could establish a state, and the Serbs would be given what they -- they wanted on a larger period. So during this period of 1994, the Serbs agreed to a number of measures to stabilise the situation, because holding so much of the territory they were content for the status quo to freeze on the ground. So they agreed to what we call the opening of Blue Routes; that is, the routes that would allow the circulation of the civilian population. They allowed the re-starting of the Sarajevo tramway. They agreed to turn on some of the electricity and water. They agreed to more cease-fires. They agreed to certain measures to limit sniping against civilians. And in general, when they agreed to these things, whether it was the turning on of the water or whether it was the limiting of the sniping attacks against civilians, they were normally able to deliver. And in that sense, 1994 was relatively quiet. Now, by the end of 1994, the Serbs - and again, they explained this to us. Mr. Krajisnik was relatively open about explaining their dilemma to us - felt that perhaps they had miscalculated, that time was not on their side, and that the Muslims were not going to capitulate under those circumstances and accept a land-for-peace agreement; and that in fact the -- although the Muslims were surrounded by their enemies, the Americans had succeeded in brokers a peace agreement with the Croats, assisted by their supporters in the United States and in the Islamic world, weapons were reaching the Bosnian Muslims. So the Serbs, in late 1994, decided that they would start to apply pressure more directly. So they -- at one point, they closed the Sarajevo air-lift, which was bringing humanitarian assistance; they increased the amounting of sniping and shelling; they cut off the electricity and water again; and they began to demonstrate their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I draw your attention to the fact that this is a 92 ter abbreviated procedure, and its purpose will be defeated by a lengthy examination-in-chief. So please have the witness give shorter answers and a more summarized procedure is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I will do that, Mr. President. Thanks for bringing that to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to the last quote clarification from the first Slobodan Milosevic transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is, Your Honours, on page 26951, and it starts on line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I will quote again and ask for clarification from your side. "One of the normal tactical principles of artillery bombardment of course is concentration of fire. You concentrate fire in order to clear ground or suppress enemy fire, in order to take it or something; whereas, the pattern of artillery fire around Sarajevo was precisely the opposite. It was a dispersion of fire. Shells would be dropped apparently randomly across the densely populated civilian areas of the city in a way that would cause a small number of casualties in a large number of places. We assumed that this was to keep the general level of terror high and to forestall any dramatic events around which an international response will coalesce." My question, and I hope for a brief answer, is that a statement which only applied to the situation in 1993, 1994, or also later after summer 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and in fact, it probably applied more later on. We prepared daily maps of where the impacts of artillery shells were, and these maps showed a huge dispersion of shells. They would sometimes be concentrated in one broad civilian area or another, but they were certainly not concentrated against what we would consider military targets, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just if I may, going back to the question the witness gave beforehand and just asking him very precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In one or two sentences to finish your answer about the deterioration of the situation in 1995, as you had mentioned it in the Slobodan Milosevic case; just two or three sentences.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: So 1994 was a relatively calm and stable year in which the Serbs thought they were achieving their objectives, and they entered into a lot of agreements which they agreed upon to stabilise the situation. Towards the end of 1994 and during 1995, they returned to a pattern of more intense use of military and non-military means against Sarajevo in order to force the Bosnian government to -- to enter into a peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland. And my last and fifth quote comes from the second day you testified, that's the 5th November, 2003, in the Slobodan Milosevic case. And my short quote comes from page 28684, and it's a quote from line 6 to line 9. And I believe it was a question by -- in cross-examination, and the cross-examiner refers you to your witness statement, and I quote: "Both sides targeted civilians; and when we could monitor sniper activity in Grbavica, it would appear that the Muslims were sniping more civilians than the Serbs." Now, can you explain what you meant by that sentence, which comes from your witness statement and which was read out in the Slobodan Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we knew much, much less about the exact number of casualties, military or civilian, on the Serb side because we didn't have access to the Serb side. So a lot of this was presumptive; that is, the Serb authorities would report to us that four children had been killed by snipers or whatever. And we would largely have to take that on its own, at face value; whereas, on the government side or inside the confrontation lines, we tended to know exactly how many people had been killed or almost exactly. We checked the morgues, we checked the hospitals, and we checked the battlefields and the streets. Now, the Serbs controlled all the high ground around Sarajevo, so they could snipe or shell from almost any position. The Bosnian government, however, had much less capacity to do so. They controlled some high buildings that overlooked parts of the Serb civilian inhabited area of Grbavica. So the fire out of the city by the Bosnian government forces tended to be concentrated from a relatively small number of high buildings overlooking Grbavica, and so I believe what I was pointing out was that in that part of the city, Grbavica, that's where the Bosnian government forces would have concentrated their sniper fire. Indeed, I used to see Bosnian government snipers moving in to take up their position in sniper-nests, just as I was going about my business in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these clarifications?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll now move on to the next phase. These are the documents I would like to have the witness refer to fairly, fairly briefly, if I may. And the first document is - and I hope I have that right - 65 ter number 2, which is a document dated the 15th August 1994, and that's the famous anti-sniping agreement. And I hope it now appears on some screen. And perhaps if the witness could return the two transcripts from the Milosevic case, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is on the screen is a reference to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have the agreement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think that's just the first page, Mr. President. If the next few pages could be added -- in fact, we do not need the translation at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that it's practice in these courts to have both original and translation displayed at the same time. If that's practice, I'm happy to have it both. If the second page of the English version could be displayed as well for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Harland, if it's big enough, can you tell us in very brief words -- sentences what this anti-sniping agreement is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps we can scroll down to the actual message.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the next page could be put on as well, which is the actual agreement. The next page is another introductory part. It mentions that the day before a British soldier had been killed, and then the next page will be the actual agreement, if that would be displayed, please. Thank you, Mr. Court deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harland, can you tell us in brief sentences what this anti-sniping agreement was about, who signed it, who was present during the signature ceremony?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, this was an effort, an initiative launched by us. Both sides had indicated that they had civilian sniping casualties. Those casualties, in general, were much higher on the Bosnian side, but there were certainly Serb casualties particularly in Grbavica. So we proposed that the sides enter into an agreement that would limit the sniping. The main argument was about paragraph 2, which is that we wanted the authority to go out and get the snipers, that if anybody violated the rules we would have freedom of movement within both sides to send quick patrols to go and intercept the snipers, either detain them or, if necessary, to kill them if they were in the act of firing. And that could not be agreed, but they -- both sides did agree to pass orders and limiting sniping and to allow us some limited monitoring and to announce it on their public media as an indication of good faith. As for who was there, I mean the -- I mean I was there, but the -- and I believe I drafted the text of the agreement and of this cover you were showing. And from the Bosnian side, Mustafa Hajrulahovic was there, Vahid Karavelic, I think, and Hasan Muratovic. The Serb side, General Milosevic, who was relatively new at that stage; and Professor Koljevic; General Tolimir; other people came and went. I think there were also, if I remember correctly, we held the negotiations at a FrenchBat facility at Sarajevo airport, so several French officers were in and out of the room. I now no longer remember exactly who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was the agreement intended to prohibit sniping that was of a defensive character, or is sniping, by definition, necessarily offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was intended to -- to limit -- prevent sniping, both against military and civilian personnel. There is sniping, if I can put it this way, that is legitimate, that is the use of marksmen to target military personnel of the opposing force at a considerable distance. And, in fact, a lot of the sniping that took place in Sarajevo was going on all the time. It was snipers from one position on one side trying to identify snipers, military personnel, on the other side. And they would engage in sort of duels, and they would move quickly from one location to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you meant wasn't intending to prohibit that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually it was, because we felt the same people were using the same weapons sometimes to engage in what you might describe as legitimate military activity; that is, activity against other uniformed military personnel. But often they were using it for, you know, indiscriminate attacks against civilians. So our agreement, in fact, tried to stop all sniping. And we even proposed that we put line-of-sight barriers using UNHCR plastic sheeting so that the snipers couldn't physically see each other or couldn't see the civilian population on the other side of the line. So the question is actually a very legitimate one, that we were trying to limit a legitimate military activity as well as the -- the attacks on civilians, just because we thought that they couldn't really be distinguished properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this, you talked about the policies of Sarajevo Romanija Corps, which was -- which actually sought to instill terror within the civil population in Bosnia with the sniping and the bombing, the shelling. But what I would like to ask you is the following: There were snipers of the government on various buildings that were on high elevation of Grbavica inhabited by the Serbs. It's in the transcript on page 15, from 23 -- lines 23 through 25. So my question is the following: Aside from this intentional policy, according to your statement, on behalf of the corps of Sarajevo Romanija very probably and, according to your statement, that it was also from the Bosnian government at this stage, according to what you have seen, could we have sought or could one have imagined that intentional sniping from Bosnian snipers against their own objectives, against their own -- could they have shot on their own targets? You didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is, of course, a -- an extremely sensitive subject, and it was a very sensitive subject at the time. It was a common allegation of the Serb side that the Bosnians were sniping against their own side. Our observations were that there were -- there were some cases of this, not a large number. Certainly more than 90 percent of the victims on the Bosnian side, when we could identify with any certainty where the shots came from, appeared to have been shot from the Serb side of the confrontation line. But there were certainly cases, as you suggest, in which Bosnian civilians on the Bosnian side of the confrontation line were shot by bullets that appeared to have originated on the Bosnian side of the confrontation line. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I have a last question about this document. What was the effect of the anti-sniping agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: There was a -- there was an immediate and sharp decline in the number of civilian sniper casualties. If I remember correctly, we thought that the command and control, particularly on the Serb side, was very strong because we had failed in our efforts to have line-of-sight barriers erected between the two sides; and yet, even so, the number of casualties fell dramatically for a certain period, I can't remember now, a month or two months or maybe three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland. Mr. President I would like to move on to the next document unless you have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next document, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Mr. Court deputy is ter number 1.982, and it's a document dated 18 August 1994, an UNPROFOR memorandum addressed to a Colonel Lugonja, subject: Anti-sniping Application Measures, a two-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, can you very briefly tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Actually, I can only see a part of it. Yeah. This is not one of the documents that I wrote. This is, in fact, a document from Sector Sarajevo; whereas, I was the political officer for Bosnia and Herzegovina headquarters. We were both in Sarajevo, but this was the subordinate sector headquarters. But this is a -- a follow-up implementation arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, it discusses in the first sentence follow-up meetings about measures of implementation of this agreement, meaning the anti-sniping agreement. Were you aware of these follow-up meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and I also was involved in some of the follow-up activities to the agreement. The agreement was also followed by some implementation agreements and a codicil to it. A number of measures designed to make it more effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can move on to 65 ter number 5, and this, in fact, might be one of the codicils you just mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 65 ter number 5, it's called codicil to the anti-sniping agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is this a document you had mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe this one was drafted by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document, and this is 65 ter number 2007. Perhaps if you can give us a brief comment about an out-going code cable, which has some relevant information about this case dated 12th September 1994. It's stated, Violation of Sarajevo Anti-sniping Agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This cable, which is appearing on my screen, is a cable from Zagreb which was UNPROFOR theatre headquarters to New York. I was at the subordinate headquarters; that is, the Bosnia and Herzegovina command in Sarajevo. So this cable would have been written using information that we provided then, but this information -- this cable was not drafted by me and would not have been seen by me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does seem correct, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document which is 65 ter number 2134.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It was drafted by Tony Banbury but emanates from the office of Victor Andreev, dated 15th November, 1994, and perhaps if you want to read the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have a comment about the authenticity of this document, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. This document was written in my presence, by my office mate, Tony Banbury, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's move on to the next document, which is number 19, a document dated 23rd November 1994, and it's dated -- it's referred to as "Code meeting with Generals Gobilliard and Milosevic, 23rd November 1994." And if you can have a look, especially at paragraph 1, Mr. Harland, especially the acronym "DMZ." Can you tell Their Honours what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, this is another document from our subordinate headquarters; that is, from the Sarajevo Sector headquarters. And it is about an effort to create a weapons-free zone around Sarajevo, which was sometimes called by NATO the total exclusion zone, but was sometimes were neutrally known as a demilitarised zone. These were -- this was a zone established in, I believe, April of 1994, after the so-called Markale 1 massacre and subject to NATO -- and following NATO threats. And the Serb compliance with it had always been rather problematic, and one of the efforts of UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo was to try to get the terms of the agreement on the demilitarisation of the Sarajevo area truly agreed to rather -- by the parties, rather than simply demanded by external actors such as the United Nations or NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move on, perhaps, to the next document. Mr. President, Your Honours, this is document 2145. And this is a type of document, Your Honours, which we will see more often in this case and Mr. Harland could perhaps -- I'm not sure whether that's the right document, though, 2145. Yes, that's the right document. Thank you very much, Mr. Court deputy?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you explain, Mr. Harland, to Their Honours what type of communication this is.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: This is a daily situation report from UNPROFOR theatre headquarters in Zagreb to New York describing the military events of the previous 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps as an example, Mr. President, Your Honours, we'll move to page 5 of this document. And if paragraph 2 -- yes, that's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I can quote paragraph 2: "Sector Sarajevo: The situation in Sarajevo was tense. There was virtually no UNPROFOR movement allowed in the BSA-controlled area, apparently as a reaction to air-strikes over the last three days." Then it moves on to: "Sniper Alley was active with numerous incidents and a heavy exchange of fire in the Holiday Inn and Grbavica areas involving three anti-tank rockets shot at the BiH police station and three others," and so on. So who provided the information for the -- the basic background information for these kind of reports, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move on to the next documents. Your Honours, this is 2158.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, any comments on this document? It's dated 10th December 1994.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. I wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, on page 6, the situation in Sarajevo, the electricity, other utilities situation for the civilian population is discussed on page 6. If we can move on to the next document, this is 2262. And we are now moving into 1995. It's a document dated 29th March 1995, especially -- in particular paragraph 1 might be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, if you have any comments.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. This was the deterioration of the security situation in Sarajevo that I was speaking about at excessive length before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just for Your Honours' benefit, from pages 5 onwards, there are a number of charts barely readable, legible. And we are not relying on these charts, obviously, just for the record. If we move on to the next document, Mr. President, Your Honours, that's 65 ter number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Luc Duchesne is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Luc Duchesne was a civil affairs officer working for me at Sector Sarajevo headquarters in the -- what we called the PTT engineering building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the next document is number 6. It dates 24th April 1995, and it's dealing with anti-sniping project, again from Mr. Luc Duchesne. It's a fairly detailed document, detailing all these various measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think you -- I believe you already discussed, you know, the plastic you used. Do you remember that --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- project?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We wanted to erect a continuous, very tall, plastic barrier, non-see-through plastic barrier so that snipers from either side would not be able to see targets on the other side of the line. But the Serbs ultimately did not agree for this to go ahead. And when we tried to put some containers, some sea containers unilaterally in the most exposed places, our troops were shot at, in fact, one of them was killed while operating a fork-lift trying to establish these barriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And shot at from --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: From the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move on to the next document which is ter number 511. It's, again, an UNPROFOR communication. The releasing officer is Colonel Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have any comments, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I can't see the text of the document. Colonel Demurenko was the Chief of Staff of our Sector Sarajevo office, an officer from the Russian Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the document could be moved up so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was is that, again, one of the communications UNPROFOR released?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. This was a communication from the subordinate Sector Sarajevo office to the UNPROFOR command office at which I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move on to the next document, which is ter number 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It dates 3rd June, 1995, and it deals on page 3 with the food situation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go to page 3. At the top, it has a reference to UNHCR bringing in flour to Sarajevo and another reference to the rapidly deteriorating situation of food in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have any comments on that, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. The -- Sarajevo was completely surrounded for most of the war. The Serbs usually let in just enough food so that people would not starve; however, at the beginning of 1995, they brought fire to bear on the airport. So the airport was no longer available for bringing in humanitarian supplies. So the only way we were able to feed the quarter of a million people of Sarajevo was by bringing convoys over Mount Igman and then over -- over a narrow corridor of Sarajevo airport that we controlled, and then the Serbs of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps would fire on us and on the humanitarian convoys we were escorting down this mountain dirt-road into the city. And so this report is about ongoing problems that we had and our efforts to protect that Igman road by barricades and fire from attacks from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps that was trying to cut off the supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move on to number 2471, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's a document dated 24th June, 1995. And, Mr. Harland, I would like you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- to draw your attention to the third paragraph, which discusses the humanitarian situation in the city, the fact that civilians had been killed at water-lines and marketplaces and negotiations to restore utilities are ongoing. Any comments, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. This would happen at times of greater political tension that the Serb military would shoot at convoys to try and stop them or would increase the sniping. It was popular to shell water -- places where people gathered for water because people had to gather there in larger numbers. Normally, people were just hiding in their apartments or in their cellars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next document might need some explanation from your side, Mr. Harland. This is 2490 and it's a document dated 30th June 1995, and it goes to Mr. Phillip Korwin. It's signed by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could go on to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The second paragraph is probably the most important, if you want to familiarise yourself, Mr. Harland, it. And please explain us, if you recall the incident, explain us what triggered your reaction.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. I was very concerned during the period of May and June and July of 2005 that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had in addition to its effort to increase the level of terror on the civilian population by cutting off the food and increasing sniping and random shelling had also begun some targeted shelling against us. And I was -- during the period this was written, I had moved from my regular job at BH command because of a shortage of personnel, and I had taken over the civil affairs office at Sector Sarajevo. And my counter-part, military counter-part, the acting sector commander and I, Colonel Meille, were very distressed at what was going on. And the Serbs would fire shells at us to limit our activity, to observe sniping and so on. And we didn't have heavy weapons, but often the Bosnian army would fire back at the Serb firing point. Now, this Phillip Korwin had -- he had protested that the Bosnian government had fired these weapons back at the Serbs from a distance that was too close to our locations, and that was -- that was correct. But it seemed to me that the basic point that he was -- missed was that they were doing that because that's the shells from the Serb side were landing right on our positions, I mean literally outside my office windows. We had shrapnel coming through the windows, and nearby Bosnian units were firing back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have only five more documents to go, and then we are completed. The next document is 2491. And while the document is being retrieved, Mr. Harland, in answering my question I think you said, or it's in the transcript, as referring to the period May and June and July 2005. I guess you meant or you might have said 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm Sorry. Yes, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a document which appears to be signed by the gentleman you just mentioned in your previous answer, Colonel Meille, and it's addressed to MAJOR-GENERAL Dragomir Milosevic. Are you familiar with this junior?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit more about the circumstances, if you can?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: During this period May and June and July of 1995, the Serb direct targeting of us and indiscriminate targeting of the city substantially intensified and also some new weapons that we had not been familiar with before were deployed, such as the slow-moving improvised rockets. And we discussed what actions, political and military, we could take. And one of the first things we agreed should be done was that there -- it should be put on record through a protest. Normally, we simply telephoned our protest or we delivered them to the liaison officer, Colonel Indjic, but sometimes we would directly approach commanders, either in Lukavica or in Pale and relay them and sometimes write these letters. And this is an example of -- of one. I should say they generally didn't do any good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, we would make the protests, but it wouldn't lead to any -- to any change of behaviour at all by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When protests were launched, letters like that, do you recall what the answer of the protestee to these protests were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Sometimes they -- the Serbs would tell us that the Bosnians had either fired out of the city or they were preparing an offensive, and so they had done these things. And we would then say, you know, if the Bosnians have launched a military effort to break out of the city, that's no justification for either targeting us or for targeting the civilian population. But they were normally not responsive. Sometimes they would also say that it was uncontrolled elements, but we -- we did not think that they were uncontrolled elements because the pattern into which they fitted was consistent with the elements that were under -- under command. And when they seemed to have a desire to limit this activity, either in the context of a political negotiation or in response to a threat from NATO, suddenly we might have 100 percent compliance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you then, Mr. Harland, from what you say, the Serbs appeared to have disputed the facts as you presented those facts to them. It's not that they promised to do something and then did not fulfil that promise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both. Sometimes they would dispute the facts. They would say that the Muslims had fired mortars at themselves, for example, but generally we were confident that this was not true. We had our own mortar-detecting radars. We had UNMOs, military UN observers on the ground so we were normally confident of the facts. But you are correct that they would sometimes dispute the facts. Then sometimes they would give an explanation, but not promise to change their behaviour because they apparently thought it was reasonable that if there had been a Bosnian military act in one area, that they could respond in this way. And the third possibility, which you've just mentioned, is that they might undertake to -- to stop the behaviour, but we didn't notice any abatement of it. And we did monitor the exact number of incoming rounds very carefully from day-to-day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's time for the adjournment. We adjourn for 20 minutes, and I would like to see the Legal Officer in my chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have five documents left, and I think we can finish fairly quickly. The first document, Mr. President, Your Honours is ter number 2503. This is a communication drafted by you, Mr. Harland, 2nd July 1995. And it deals on the third page on top of it with an incident on 25th of June when a 16-year-old boy was killed while riding his bicycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you were fairly close to that incident, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you actually seen the incident?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: The incident took place just around the corner from where I was. I was -- in fact, there are many, many sniping incidents all the time, and I didn't always write up each one of them in our -- our reports. I mentioned this one only because in -- as a specific incident because I happened to be walking down the street from the main UNPROFOR headquarters; that is, the building which is now the US embassy in Sarajevo I think on -- is it on Djure Djakovic Street as it was called then down the street. And I heard a small number of shots, and then there was a -- a commotion. I think I was near the bottom of the street and then I turned the -- near the Kino, the cinema Radnik, and I turned at the Alipasino mosque, and there was a bicycle on the ground. And people were trying to pull away a young boy who had been hit in the head and who was dead. And there was always a mixture of fear and panic, worry when people tried to help because you never really knew where the shot had -- often didn't know where the shot had come from, and people were afraid of more. And people were indicating to -- that there was, in fact, a building. I think it was the one we called the white building in Grbavica as -- which was, in fact, visible from that point which seemed to have been the firing location, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And on -- who held that territory on which the white building was located in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That was a Serb-held position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move on to the next document. This is 103. It dates 8th July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you were the drafter, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 103, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't have a 103 in e-court. I have a 28 and the next document is 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yeah. It's a document dated 8th July 1995. The ERN is R0024208.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Otherwise, we'll just go over it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I cannot locate the document with that ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The next one is 2597. And I believe we have talked about one of these releasing officers before; it's Colonel Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Colonel Demurenko, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Colonel Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I believe he was Chief of Staff of the sector headquarters for Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's, again, a standard UNPROFOR communication?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's move to the next document, which is the second-to-last, 2629. And it's an outgoing code cable dated 5th September 1995. And the first paragraph deals with the fact that there was "no evidence of significant heavy weapon withdrawal from the Sarajevo area." Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: This document is a cable from UNPROFOR theatre headquarters in Zagreb to New York. So I would not have seen this document at the time of drafting, but my office probably would have provided the information on which it was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember the dispute about the withdrawal of heavy weaponry from the Sarajevo area that occurred in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last document, Mr. President, Your Honours, is document number 3. And it's titled, "First Meeting on the Implementation of the Cease-fire Agreement of 5th October 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it lists you, Mr. Harland, as being present, a few other personnel from UNPROFOR, and a few personalities from the side of Republika Srpska; Mr. Milosevic, Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic. Do you recall these meetings, series of meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: In the weeks prior to this communication, the Government of Croatia had launched a military attack against the Croatian Serbs; Operation Oluja, Operation Storm. And the Croatian-Serb forces had collapsed in complete defeat. Croatian government forces had then surged into Bosnia and were on a military campaign against the Bosnian Serbs. And the Bosnian Serbs feared that they were on the brink of a complete military collapse. We knew this because General Mladic came to us in great alarm and said that he wanted quickly to accelerate the peace talks that were going on under the auspices of the Americans at that point. And the Bosnians who were on the advance for the first time in the war said that they could not consider a full end to the war unless the Serbs restored electricity and gas and food to the people of Sarajevo, sort of lifted the sort of cycle of terror, which the Serbs had already said they didn't really have it within their power to lift so easily. And yet, they -- here was the agreement where suddenly the Serbs wanted it to happen and, indeed, it did happen. The gas and electricity supplies suddenly increased and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. President, Your Honours is:

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You have met the accused, Mr. Dragomir Milosevic, his predecessor, General Galic. You met General Tolimir and other Bosnian Serb generals. Can you tell Their Honours your impression about these personalities?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I met General Milosevic in the context of meetings, as I had his predecessor General Galic. But I didn't have a personal relationship with him as, you know, I did perhaps with General Mladic or Professor Koljevic or even General Tolimir. So I don't -- did not have a strong impression of General Milosevic as a personality. But I did -- I did have the impression that from seeing him in the negotiations on the sniper agreement in 1994 that he was a forceful and commanding personality, rather more commanding presence, perhaps, than his predecessor, General Galic. But I did not know General Milosevic personally, I could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do we have that document, 103? If it just could be displayed, because it's again drafted by Mr. Harland. Document number 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Harland, that's a document drafted by you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And on page 2, Your Honours, one of the subjects discussed are attacks on civilians, but we don't need to go into that because it's mentioned there and Mr. Harland testified about that in detail. That completes, Mr. President, Your Honours, examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, there are two matters I take up. First, the Chamber will not accept that the Prosecutor can spend an hour and 40 minutes in a 92 ter proceeding. The 92 ter proceeding is designed to facilitate the admission of evidence from previous proceedings without going through an examination-in-chief. It's not a new procedure; it's really 89(F) codified. And I have been in trials in which we have used 89(F), and the Prosecutor spends no more than 10, 15, or 20 minutes introducing the witness. So an hour and 40 minutes is unacceptable. It defeats the purpose of the procedure, which is to expedite the proceedings. I allowed you to go on, as this was the first witness, but I'm to say that the Chamber will not allow that length of time for the introduction of a 92 ter. I'm resisting trying hard not to say examination-in-chief, because it is not examination-in-chief. The procedure is designed to avoid examination-in-chief. The other matter is that I've decided to admit -- to deal with the admission of the exhibits now rather than at the end of cross-examination, because I think that would facilitate the cross-examiner's citation of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I accept your point about the procedural issues. It was also the first witness from our side which -- and also my first witness under this rule. So I do apologise if I went over -- over the examinable time, and we will certainly abide by your ruling in future. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we deal with the admission of the exhibits now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you want me to read out the numbers I'm proposing to tendering or is it the court officer who is doing that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have the court officer. You'll read the admission of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The transcript dated 18th September, 65 ter number 02815, will be Exhibit P1. The memo dated 23rd of November, 65 ter number 00019 will become Exhibit P8. The daily sitrep 24th of November, 65 ter number 02145, will become Exhibit P9. The weekly sitrep report dated 10th of December, 65 ter number 02158, will become Exhibit P10. The agreement dated 29th of March, 65 ter number 02262, will become Exhibit P11. The report dated the 15th of April, 65 ter number 00022, will become Exhibit P12. The memo dated 24th of April, 65 ter number 6 will become Exhibit P13. The UNPROFOR message dated 22nd May, 65 ter number 00011, will become Exhibit P14. The UNPROFOR memo dated 3rd June, 65 ter number 00104, will become Exhibit P15. The UNPROFOR memo dated 24th of June, 65 ter number 02471, will become Exhibit P16. The UNPROFOR memo of 30th June, 65 ter number 02490, will become Exhibit P17. The protest letter dated 30th of June will -- 65 ter number 02491, will become Exhibit P18. The UNPROFOR memo dated 2nd of July, 65 ter number 02503, will become Exhibit P19. The UNPROFOR memo dated 8th of July, 65 ter number 3, which also had an ERN number of R0024208, that will become Exhibit P20. The UNPROFOR sitrep of 28th August, 65 ter number 02597, will become Exhibit P21. The cable dated 5th of September, 65 ter number 02629, becomes Exhibit P22. The cable dated 5th of September -- I'm sorry, I just did that. The minutes dated 5th of October, 65 ter number 00 -- sorry, was the 65 ter number 00 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's 3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct. 0003 becomes Exhibit P23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. There is a technical problem. I just needed the lectern. I took part, Your Honours, on several occasions in certain proceedings in this Tribunal, and I was in a different situations. But this is the first time that I'm taking part in the procedure of this nature where we are dominated by technology and electronics. We made a tremendous effort to try to overcome these difficulties, and hopefully today we shall manage to function properly and do our duty as required. But before I start my cross-examination, I would kindly ask you that during today's sitting, towards the end of it, rather, you allocate a few minutes for certain procedural matters that I would like to raise before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Harland. We are meeting now for the first time -- for the third time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I would like to express my pleasure that you are still in good health. What I would like to say is that I will do my best to ask my questions as directly as possible; and as you already know, we should try if possible and whenever possible to give us the briefest possible answers. If -- preferably, if you can just say yes or no. There are a couple of topics that I would like to cover related to the documents that you had prepared, and I will try to be as direct as possible. The first issue that I'm interested in and what the Chamber should hear about, you said that you arrived in Sarajevo in the capacity of -- in your capacity towards the end of May, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, the end of May or the beginning of June, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you are well aware that the Security Council Resolution dated, I think, the 4th of May, number 824 referred to protected zones, and one of those protected zones was Sarajevo. And I presume that the United Nations had sent their representative, among other things, in order to implement this on the ground which was contained in the resolution, 824. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You've asked three questions there. I would like you to ask the questions separately, and please bear that in mind, but I will allow the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You're right about when I arrived and you are correct about the date of the passage of Resolution 824 and you are also correct that 824 became a part of the mandate of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that upon your arrival, as one of your primary tasks, you had a duty to secure or ensure free movement of people?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. It was a mandated task of UNPROFOR to try to secure freedom of movement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You talked to a large number of Serbs and -- those Serbs whom you met in Sarajevo, and they expressed their desire to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that, are you primarily referring to those Serbs who were in the neighbourhoods under the control of the Muslim military forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And those who wanted to leave were unable to do so because they were not allowed by the Muslim authorities to do that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That is correct. That is certainly one of the main reasons they could not leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If that is correct, that they were not allowed to leave, does that constitute a serious violation of international conventions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, but it was certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer. Don't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I appreciate that. I am not going to go through this transcript because that will take too much time; but at the last trial, Mr. Harland responded directly in affirmative to this question and it can be found in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My second subject is somewhat similar. Before you came to Sarajevo, were you familiar with the fact that in Sarajevo, before the outbreak of the conflict, between 150 and 180.000 Serbs had lived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Was I familiar with that fact before I arrived in Sarajevo? I don't recall. Perhaps I was not familiar with that, but became aware of it on my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you arrived in Sarajevo, or maybe afterwards, were you informed about the existence about a certain national Serbian project of ethnic cleansing that was being implemented solely by the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No. It was not our impression that ethnic cleansing was solely done by the Serbian side, and that was not my personal experience. I travelled extensively around the country. And, in fact, the first example of ethnic cleansing that I saw was I was in the city, small city, of Kakanj when it fell to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was fighting against the Croats. And the Croat population was being physically removed house by house by a unit called the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But when you arrived in Sarajevo, did -- were you not -- did you not become aware yourself, in light of the information that you just mentioned, and did you learn that at the time when you arrived, only 40.000 Serbs were living there at the moment when you arrived -- means that at the moment when you arrived about 140.000 Serbs had already left.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I don't now remember the exact number, but that is approximately our understanding as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There's another thing. A while ago you spoke about the pressure when you responded to the question of my learned colleague Waespi about the pressures that were being exerted, and you also mentioned that they were holding 70 percent of the territory throughout the war and that as a result they launched or adopted a so-called offensive strategy, so to speak. But did you know and did you ever find out about the fact that before the war, before the war broke out, 65 percent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was owned by the Serbs according to title deeds, according to land registers, as an inalienable right which is related to right to the private property. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That was an assertion that was frequently made to us by our Bosnian Serb colleagues, but my own office did some research on the matter and we disagreed with that finding by a Serbian group. We found that about 30 percent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was entirely uninhabited and was the property of the state. It is true that the Serbs were more preponderant in the rural areas and so the areas under the communist system had some level of private title. The Serbs did hold more of them in the rural areas. In the urban areas which were more inhabited by the Muslim population, there would often be more socially owned -- so-called socially owned properties. But the general statement that the Serbs owned 65 percent of Bosnia is a certainly misleading and, in my view, basically an inaccurate statement about the distribution of population in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, you just mentioned yourself the word "communism." Do you know that in the communist system, property had been confiscated from people who owned it and became state property. Only now, after all the reforms that had been implemented, the situation is being reversed and people are getting back their property, regardless of what had happened before, and that the property owned by the Serbs during the communist era was confiscated from them but left in the land registry. Were you aware of that? If not, just tell us so?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware that title to land in Bosnia-Herzegovina over a period of 130 years had changed dramatically; sometimes forcibly, sometimes voluntarily. At the moment of -- in the late 19th century, it was overwhelming Muslim owned. There was a wave of confiscations and then there was substantial Serb holdings; and then after 1945, there was a large amount of state or so-called social holdings. Yes. We were very aware that title had shifted dramatically over a period of several decades, and that's one of the reasons that this figure of the Serbs owned 65 percent of Bosnia seemed to us an essentially unscientific and more propagandistic statement than actually an accurate reflection of the distribution of population in Bosnia-Herzegovina; though it is true that the Bosnian Serbs by and large were more preponderant in rural areas and, therefore, tended to have more land. That is true as a general fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the question that you put, if I understood it correctly, is that 65 percent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was owned by the Serbs according to title deeds, but ownership of property is -- is a different concept from ownership of territory, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. But most of the Serbs remained in the area that they owned precisely around Sarajevo, what Mr. Harland just mentioned, and I wanted to ask him about that. These rural areas around Sarajevo were held by the Serbs or owned by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but you're speaking of property, private property?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, about property, private property. That is correct. Exclusively about the property -- private populate, that's what I am referring to. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't want that to be confused with ownership of the territory, with questions of sovereignty of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, that's a matter of -- it's a legal matter and there's no need to dwell on that. I perfectly understand what you are saying and I take note of that, and we shall address this issue in the course of the forthcoming proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Though, the statement is still wrong even as -- even as framed like that. If you were to take all of the private property deeds of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of the 1991 census and put them all together, those title deeds owned by people declaring themselves of Serb nationality would certainly not have represented 65 percent of the surface area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in fact, this has been badly manipulated. And in fact, I wonder, sir, President Milosevic even gave me a map which coloured the Sarajevo area according to which population was preponderant and owned which parts, and so there is just a little green strip in the valley of Sarajevo. And it covered the whole of Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica, which are essentially uninhabited areas with the colouring of Serb ethnicity. These were, we felt, essentially manipulations, propagandistic statements rather than statements of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland. Let us move now on to another subject matter. You said that you arrived in Sarajevo as a civil servant of -- for the United Nations. Is it true - and I can see from the reports and from what you said today - that you were involved in military issues as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
