utterances.text: My responsibility was to report on all the mandated areas of UNPROFOR's work; that included military as well as political and humanitarian. That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your earlier testimony, you said that Sarajevo was in the valley and that the Serbs were on hilltops around it. You said the same today.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask this map that Mr. Waespi had already submitted, 0044-1766, that's the UNPROFOR mark, to be displayed on screens, please. It was shown in the opening statement. We don't have it on e-court, as I believed that it was. I don't have it. I don't have a copy for Mr. Harland either. If one copy can be given to Mr. Harland, can we try somehow because this is very inconvenient. I had other maps as well, but I believe that I can use this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harland has been given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 004401676.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is marked number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we can't see it on our monitors, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can move it a little bit towards east.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, Kiseljak where you work, it was in the valley, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No, Kiseljak is not on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I wanted to ask you something else. Since you said what you stated, and we all heard you, did you ever go within this circle here? On this map you can see this yellow line which indicates the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina positions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the red line indicates the Army of the 1st Corps of Republika Srpska. This is the demarcation line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, at a certain date. I couldn't tell you what date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at this area here, were you ever at Colina Kapa which is on -- to the east. It's a hill about 966 metres high. Did you hear about that ever Colina Kapa? It's not marked on this map, but it's somewhere here to the east and near Debelo Brdo. And this hill called Colina Kapa is 966 metres high. Were you ever there or weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I was at Debelo Brdo, which is marked on this point, which was the -- one of the higher positions occupied by --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I was saying I did visit Debelo Brdo, which you mentioned, and which is marked on this map and which is an area higher up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you point that out for us, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is here. It is a hill, a reasonably high hill, that was heavily contested between the Bosnian army and the Serb army. And UNPROFOR also had a position on the hill that was regularly under attack, but I believe that the question is trying to ask me whether I was aware that there was some high ground within the confrontation lines as marked on this map. And yes, of course, I'm aware that there was some high ground, but essentially this is a valley which is overwhelming dominated from the north and south and east faces of the valley by higher ground held by the Serbs. So we could probably just move on if we -- if I accept that perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Debelo Brdo, Mr. Harland, is 800 metres high, and Colina Kapa around 1.000 metres. Did you ever go to Mojmilo? Can you please look to the left a bit. It's a very long hill, and the altitude is 680 metres. From Mojmilo, one can have control on both sides towards the Serbian-populated places. Can you just say yes, that you went to this hill and that it's a dominant hilltop over all the other surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's move to the north. There's only one named here, which is marked, and it's Zuc. You know that Zuc is 830 metres high. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: It's certainly a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A little bit to the east there's the Oric hill, which is nearly 900 metres high. Did you ever go there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wouldn't like to go on. There are a large number of other positions, but it's not necessary to bother this witness with this. So other people who are more familiar with the terrain will speak about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would like to see the last hill, the Oric hill, where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little to the right, lower than Zuc; that hill is 876 metres high, and nearby is Volujak, which is 824 metres high. All these hills were held by the Muslims within the yellow line; therefore, the full control on these higher-ground positions of Sarajevo was there. Can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: It is certainly fair to say that from the north slope of Zuc, which was controlled by the Bosnian army, they were able to look down into Serb-held Vogosca. That is true. So there was -- if your point is that there was some high ground that was controlled by the Bosnia-Herzegovina army which overlooked some Serb-held territory, that is true. I don't think it negates the general proposition that Sarajevo lies in a valley and that the floor of that valley was controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And these surrounding hills on the whole were controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The last two hills that you mentioned, we haven't been able to find them on the map. Have you seen them, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Zuc feature, which is the principal high ground controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina just north of Sarajevo, is marked on -- on our map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- here, and the other subordinate features are not marked. And Zuc, I did visit and can confirm that it is high ground that overlooks Serb-held territories. The other smaller features, some of them I have visited and some of them I have not visited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Vogosca was a community which prior to the war had a Muslim preponderant population, but it was taken very early in the war by the Serbs. And it had a couple of valuable factories in it for ammunition and motor vehicles. And the Muslim population was killed or expelled, but the Muslims, through the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were able to control high ground that overlooked Vogosca. So what the honourable colleague says is correct, that the Serb population, the Serb people who either had previously lived in Vogosca or who came then to serve or work in Vogosca were within the field of sight of Bosnian small-arms fire. So he is right in saying that there was some exceptions to the general statement that the Muslims were in the valleys and the Serbs controlled the high ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to point on the map, even though they are not marked, where those are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are not. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President Robinson, Vogosca is marked here all up to the north, and it's in a valley. From Zuc, it can be fully controlled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oric is next to Zuc, and it's even higher; it's 876. It's not marked here, but, Your Honours, you will be able to see this is an incomplete map, and of course I have no need to insist upon this further. With other witnesses, we are going to point to the number of these hills within this yellow circle line overlooking the valley. For now, I think that Mr. Harland has painted a clear picture to the best of his knowledge. However, in order for the Chamber to understand better, Grbavica -- it says here Hrasno, Debelo Brdo, and Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this area there, if you can see it on the map, between Debelo Brdo and Hrasno. Grbavica is situated in a valley. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is the one part of the urban heart of Sarajevo, which was controlled by the Bosnian Serb forces. And like the rest of the urban area of Sarajevo, it lies principally in a valley. It actually flows down from higher ground, known as Vrace, down to right the valley of the Miljacka River a kilometre or two below. But, principally, the higher buildings, the most densely populated area was, as in the rest of Sarajevo, was actually on the valley floor. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And let us finish this part. Let us look at the map. On this specific spot, you can see that the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina surround Grbavica from three sides. Is that right? And that this is something that can absolutely be seen. It is at this spot that Grbavica was encircled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it fair to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That is correct. It was surrounded on three sides by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not wish to belabour the point. There are other such spots, but, Mr. Harland, let's look at Nedzarici. You know very well where they are placed. Can you show Nedzarici for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. It's on -- can you see where I'm indicating on this map? I'll move the map a little bit. If you come north from the airport, you find the small settlement of Nedzarici, which comes from the airport side in a triangle with the tip of the triangle almost at the famous Oslobodjenje newspaper building. It was a famous point of much exchange of fire throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, for instance, when we are discussing Nedzarici, whether Nedzarici was encircled throughout where this line runs and that members of the Army of Republika Srpska could barely have this one corridor as their way out. For the rest, Nedzarici was surrounded by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on all the other sides?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also discussed roads. One of your last duties involved roads. When you discussed the matter in the investigative stage, in the minutes of the 9th of February, 10th of February, and so on and so forth in your statement, back in 1998, I can show it to you and you can confirm to me whether this is true - that's at page 7 in the English version - you stated: "The Serbs were unable to travel the Ilidza-Lukavica route." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That is correct. I mean, I don't have the statement. Oh, here it is. That is a correct statement of fact; but to get from Ilidza to Lukavica, they had to travel a very long way around into Eastern Bosnia and back. Yeah, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show distance from Ilidza, and can you show the route where it runs, and you said it was just several kilometres long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I understand also that others have on the screen what I'm indicating to on mine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it's not marked. Oh, here is the suburb of Ilidza and over here is the suburb of Lukavica. These were both Serb-controlled areas, and they're only a couple of kilometres apart. But as you can see, there was Bosnian-held government territory in between. So in order to get from Ilidza to Lukavica or vice versa, any traveller would have to take a very circuitous route east of Sarajevo into the mountainous territory of Eastern Bosnia, and then come back in safety away from the confrontation lines from the south and east and into Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you are of the opinion that the Serbs did not care that much about the roads as the Bosniaks did?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs were not surrounded. I mean, there was no siege. There was no -- these areas were not surrounded, and so they had some access; whereas, the -- the people of Sarajevo, a quarter of a million or whatever, they were completely surrounded. They dug a small tunnel out of the city from Dobrinja to Butmir which allowed people to go in single file and very small numbers. So the Serbs and the Bosnians were in completely different situations. And whenever we were able to measure the -- the humanitarian situation in terms of average hours of electricity or water or the average intake of food or the number of casualties for the -- per population unit, the situation within the confrontation lines was, you know, obviously vastly worse than the situation outside the confrontation lines held by the Serbs. But if your point is that there were also some difficulties for the Serbs, either in areas exposed to fire or because they had to take long routes to get to where they wanted to go, that's true; but that was a different and altogether lesser order of problem in terms of human need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me present you with an example which has to do with your statement that the Serbs did not care that much about the roads. You spoke of the short distance between Nedzarici and Grbavica -- that is to say, between Lukavica and Ilidza. Do you know -- are you aware of the fact that there was a hospital there for the Serbs, and did you know that the hospital was unable to provide medical care for people who were seriously injured? Are you aware of this? Can you confirm that this is true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and, in fact, the people in Lukavica used other medical facilities, that is correct, which is not at all to say that their medical facilities were --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you do confirm that there was this hospital and that it wasn't intended for seriously injured. When the need arose for a seriously wounded person to be transported to a better-quality hospital, one had to skirt this yellow and red lines, some 180 -- some 90 to 100 kilometres to reach an adequate hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Sir, if you're trying to make a comparison between life inside and outside the confrontation line, it's impossible. I lived there throughout this period. There were some difficulties outside --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Robinson, I should like my question to be answered. I'm fully respectful of all that was happening in the valley. I'm not going into that matter. I'm raising the matter of roads. I'm not talking about military issues. I'm talking about these specific problems concerning those who were seriously injured and who had to travel the distance, and because of the fact that they had to travel the long distance they died along the way. Is that true, please say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, please respond.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the tunnel. I'd like you ask you, in connection with the tunnel, you spoke about this in the investigation stage in your statement. And I'm not sure if you have one in front of you now. And I'm talking about page 20, the last paragraph, and the first paragraph of page 21, or rather, the paragraph starts as the last one on page 20 and the first one on page 21. There, Mr. Harland, you discuss your meetings with General Delic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You stated there: "Delic did not have good command and control over his troops in Sarajevo and outside Sarajevo very little." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That was our impression, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say: "I would say that he had only limited control of forces in Sarajevo." Is that correct? And to the east of the Presidency, in particular?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That was certainly true in the earlier status of the war; but as time wore on, the command and control arrangements in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina improved somewhat in our view; though they were probably never as good as the command and control arrangements in the Army of Republika Srpska in our view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what the tunnel made possible, because you said here that once the tunnel was made, the tunnel that connected Sarajevo with Central Bosnia, the matters improved. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave in the Slobodan Milosevic case, you stated - this is in French, and you will have to confirm this so that I do not go on searching for this in the English version - you said that Karadzic and the Serbs tolerated the existence of the tunnel because it made possible communication, food, and medical supplies, and so on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic once said to me I -- we were talking about the tunnel, and he said to me, "You know, we could -- we could destroy it, but we're going to let the Muslims breathe." And it confirmed our view that the Serb intention was to inflict, you know, terror and suffering on Sarajevo but not actually to starve everybody to death. They could have, in fact, cut off all the food and water and probably forced the actually surrender of Sarajevo at certain points, but they chose not to and they chose to allow the existence of this tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to present you with a document, which is dated the 7th of October, 1994, and marked --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have your assistance in this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an outgoing dispatch message addressed to Annan. And in connection with the meeting with Karadzic and Mladic, I would like to show you paragraph 5 of the document under B2, which can be found at page 3, page 3. 001-4722-R001-4731. This is the 65 ter document number 1. Item 5, under B, or rather, item 5, B2. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No. No. I think this is a paragraph immediately before D, so it must be paragraph C. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We have items A and B under 5, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's on page 2, the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the following was noted in the report, in the middle: "On Sarajevo as a whole, Dr. Karadzic outlined the following conditions," and then some matters are being mentioned; and then concerning the tunnel: "The tunnel beneath Sarajevo should be covered up and placed under the control of UNPROFOR." So he never agreed to having the tunnel function. In other words, this is contrary to what you're saying, that he agreed with it. Because at this particular meeting, he asked for the tunnel to be covered up, filled up.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yeah, I was at this meeting. Yes. The tunnel always --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is enough for me. Time will pass quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you agreeing that this contradicts what you said before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I -- not at all. Dr. Karadzic contradicted himself, which he did all the time, by the way. He's a very flamboyant, very charming character, but he's not at all consistent. And I believe that he was under pressure from his military people to close the tunnel and to take a harder line. His military advisor, in particular General Tolimir, was constantly pushing Dr. Karadzic to push us to close the tunnel because it ran under territory we controlled. But Karadzic, when he spoke to us in private, didn't exhibit great concern about it. And he, in fact, was much aware than his military commanders that if he pushed UNPROFOR too far or the Bosnian civilians too far, that could provoke a NATO intervention which would be bad for the Serbs. So Karadzic was himself zigzagging on this issue and on many others I should say, like the provision of food to Sarajevo and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Under item 6, if I can direct your attention to this, this is precisely what you're saying, that the military authorities insisted on something quite else; and then here it is stated what Mr. Mladic said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, this is on page 4, item 6, for the court deputies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mladic firmly protested against the fact that the ABiH infantry used the tunnel to go out of Sarajevo and attack. Is it true that when the airport became operational in mid-1994, the ABiH used the tunnel to carry out various missions out of Sarajevo and to get back to Sarajevo again. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, but the date of -- which you gave was not right. The airport was opened in 1992, and the tunnel was dug by the Bosnians I believe in 1993. But your statement about what the tunnel was used for, which meant that it was including for military purposes to conduct attacks against the Serbs in other areas and then to bring back troops, that is correct that it is one of the purposes for which it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I may have been mistaken in that regard. However, at the time when the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was Dragomir Milosevic, the tunnel was constantly operational from August 1994 onwards. Are you aware of the fact that the tunnel was more than 700 metres long?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the tunnel had a cable that was running through it and that electricity supplies were restored to Sarajevo from the Neretva; that was in late 1994 when the cable provided more or less sufficient energy supplies?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I can, of course, put this to you. This is something that Alija Izetbegovic stated in his book. You haven't seen the book?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I have. I've read the book, but I'm surprised you're quoting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm compelled to, because in his book he wrote that thousands of tons of weapons and ammunition were brought in through the tunnel into Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it correct that he said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's correct that he said it, and it's correct that it was true. It's a fact. We used to try to monitor the flow of goods. There was an awful lot of black marketeering. The brigade commander, the Bosnian brigade commander on the Butmir side I think his name was Prevljak, he was we believed heavily engaged in black marketing. But there was also a flow of weapons and of military personnel because Sarajevo had a large base of population, and they would send troops out to fight in other areas. The weapons, on the other hand, were outside of Sarajevo, they would be given weapons, and then they would send troops back in for -- to their homes and often send weapons in as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And why would you be surprised that Mr. Tapuskovic is quoting from Alija Izetbegovic's book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't realise -- didn't realise that he considered it a reliable source for a narrative of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I'm glad to hear that he does, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I can only give you my impression. To me, that is the most important thing, to be able to hear something like that from the person that headed the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You spoke of black marketeering. Were Muslim citizens able to use the tunnel to leave the town whenever they wished to and to come back?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. If they were well-connected or if they paid a fee, yes, some were able to. But the great majority of -- or many of the population who would rather not have endured the siege were -- were not able to use the tunnel to escape the suffering of the siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's time for the break. Do you have one more question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs never. They either had to pay hefty sums of money to go out; and then even if they managed to get out, it would so happen that they would be killed at the end of the road. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No. Some Serbs did use the tunnel. Generally, Serbs -- Serbs who were trying to leave Sarajevo for good, permanently, they generally would not use the tunnel, because the tunnel was connecting it to other Bosnian government-held areas. If they wanted to leave Sarajevo, they tended to cross the front line in order to go to Serb-held territory, Lukavica or Ilidza. And there they would normally have to pay some money to a Bosnian commander and sometimes they would also have to pay money to a Serb local military unit, and then they could escape that way. But some Serb businessmen who stayed on the Bosnian side during the war, they did use the tunnel to buy goods outside where prices were cheaper and then bring them back and sell them at a larger profit. Serb -- Bosnian businessmen of Serb nationality known to me were involved in this black market trade, along with Bosnian Muslims. Black market was a major feature of the war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, let us move now on to military questions, as it were; particularly, the problems that arose in the aftermath of the tragic event of Markale on the 5th of February, 1994. I'm not going to remind you about this. For the Chamber, I think it will be interested that everything that was undertaken in order to calm down the situation, and in that respect I would like to ask you a few questions. You know that the agreement was concluded - I would not go into many details right now - and that this agreement was reached for a large number of heavy weaponry on both sides to be placed under the control of UNPROFOR. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it was done in a certain sense, as you explained page 28674, line 10-21. I would not go back to that, because it will take too much time. I would like only to focus on one thing. I don't know if it is true that part of the weapons, so my first question was: Was part of the weapons at certain points placed under the direct control of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: They were placed under the monitoring of UNPROFOR, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And was a considerable amount of weapons replaced or moved 20 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I will present to you a document drafted by you. Victor Andreev sent it to Sergio De Mello. It's dated the 17th of February. This should be our exhibit, and I just omitted a while ago that the previous document be marked as Defence document number 1. That's 7th of October, 1994; that would be Exhibit Number 1 if you permit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit that as Exhibit Number 1 for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the document dated the 17th of February; In English version last paragraph on page 1, which I'm going to read to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have this document in front of you, sir? So page 1 immediately after the introduction which shows who had drafted the document. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I have that cover page, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Last paragraph on this cover page reads as follows: "The Serbs are cooperating more than they had been ever before. Heavy weaponry is silent and a number of long-standing problems have been solved." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Another question, and I must ask you that because it relates to this document and I want to avoid going back to it again later. In English version, that's page 3, immediately after the passage which says "Rump BH." So page 3 of the English version towards the end under the heading "the Rump BH," the last-but-one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "The BH authorities of Sarajevo appear to be diverting even more food than usual away from those that it intended to, perhaps less than one-third of the aid brought into the city. It is not entirely clear what is happening to the balance. Some resurfaces on the black market and some of it is diverted to the military; most, however, cannot be accounted for." So this is what you wrote in your report. Does this mean that these enormous amounts that were arriving in Sarajevo in order to aid the civilians were diverted elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: A large amount, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now read a piece on page 28657 of the transcript line 2-6, if we can please have this on your monitor. Has this been found, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. It has been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reads as follows: "Towards the end of 1994, it seems that the Serbs genuinely wanted the stabilisation on the situation in Sarajevo and they ceased fire. In fact, they did that" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. It's not on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And am I correct that you're referring to his testimony in Slobodan Milosevic, to the transcript page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that is the second day he testified?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's been tendered, yes. 28657, 2-6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just wait until it has been identified and found so that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. That's the transcript from the trial in the proceedings against Slobodan Milosevic. I apologise if I omitted to say that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And do you have a 65 ter number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should it be admitted under 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 65 ter, if I can assist, is 02186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you must make sure that you have all of the relevant data for easy identification of your documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. I was sure that I had the correct page, and that's what I have from the transcript from the Slobodan Milosevic trial, page 28657.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the line number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you repeat the page and the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 28657, lines 2 to 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very important to me, and I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So by the end of February 1994, the Serbs did seem genuinely to want a stabilisation of the situation around Sarajevo, and they did stop shooting. And, in fact, they did so. They reduced the amount of fire coming from their side of the confrontation line from February of 1994, right through till the autumn of 1994 to a very low level. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this period - and I wouldn't refer to the transcript any longer because I believe you remember, and you confirmed that in Slobodan Milosevic trial - that between 10th February and 27th April 1994, there were 318 cease-fires by the Muslims, to which you responded approximately. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact number, but that is approximately right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid any further confusion, I have to refer to the following on page 28 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just -- it's not clear to me what you mean by 318 cease-fires by the Muslims, to which you responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 318 times the Muslims fired from their positions in violation of the truce and cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's different from what is on the transcript. So they breached the cease-fire 318 times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that occasioned a response from UNPROFOR. Is that so, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It elicited protests from us, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me read this in French. [Interpretation] "We were concerned about the fact that certain -- about certain elements, that's for sure, about the fact that some Muslim leaders did not want to stabilise the situation all around Sarajevo. This was extremely frustrating for General Rose."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If he could give a reference to the transcript page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you in the English version. That's page 28659, lines 15 to 18. It's a very brief statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that sounds correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, let me present to you now a document dated 18th September 1994; just a portion of this document, on 65 ter list, there's not the entire document. This is just a part of this document. It's on the 65 ter list -- no, it's not on the 65 ter list; only part of it is but not this particular part. It refers to the protection forces of UNPROFOR related to the report on the shelling which took place on the 18th of September, 1994. This part was tendered as 1429; part of this document was entered under 65 ter with the number 1429. And this is going to be our exhibit, but I omitted, Your Honour, to tender previously two other exhibits. So these are all the documents that we are tendering into evidence that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, would you just mention them so we can give them an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult now to do it post factum. I'll do it at the end for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does -- this part of the document is before the witness. This is 0026-3949 and 0026-3950. That's the report. Can you see it, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to this document, it is clearly shown on one side are activities by the ABiH army and on the right-hand side were activities by the Bosnian Serbs on the 18th of September. So look at this. The activities carried out by the Bosnian army started at 1715 hours, and the number of shells is given; then 30 -- 10, 30, 30, 30, 30, 40, 30, and so on and so forth until 1850 and, or rather, 1907, at which time a response came from the Serbian side; whereas, the shelling from the Bosnian side continued; and then the Serb shelling ceased at 1814, whereas, the Bosnian shelling continued until 2049 hours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what it says here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So please look at the next page on this report, which is contained in this document. It reads: "This attack had two likely objectives: To block the Serbian logistic road in order to obtain a release of the Serbian pressure on the Bosnian logistic road through Mount Igman to -- to provoke the Serbs to make a mistake and open fire at the town for the president, Izetbegovic, to give a strong argument for negotiating a lifting of the embargo by the USA. At the same time, the Bosnian opened aversionary fire in the eastern suburb near the coordinate 9358 with the intention possibly to simulate the attack towards the east along the road to Pale." Do you know about this document, and is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I didn't write this document, but it sounds like a plausible account of that incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now move on to the next document which was drafted by you only two days later, on the 20th of September. You wrote it and Victor Andreev forwarded it to Sergio De Mello. It is, again, part of 65 ter number 2230.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this the document which is now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, but I can't still see the page that I intend to quote from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is that page? Page 2230.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last two numbers are 4232.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, if I can assist, Mr. President, and colleague from the Defence, the next page is in fact the document drafted by Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you report about a meeting held in Pale. As far as I can see here, on page 1, the message was that you had a meeting with Karadzic and that he made an angry remark about the Bosnian attack on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is paragraph 2. Mr. Harland, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 7, after the meeting in the Presidency in Sarajevo, it says here that you reported that President Izetbegovic was absolutely contrite about Saturday's attack and promised, in front of General Delic, that there would be no repetition of the incident. He stated that orders had been passed to Bosnian soldiers on the ground not to respond to provocations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, it was the Bosnian side who was provoking. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: He also promised that Bosnian forces would stop their attacks on the Serb supply route around Sarajevo. Is that correct, too?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, though not everything President Izetbegovic promised was always implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have a document dated the 2nd of October, Major Fraser's report for the 2nd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 65 ter 2055. The mouse is not working on our desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do we have the document now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, you don't have it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, I hope these are initial growing pains, because I would have to say that right now the system is slower than the previous one where we used hard documents. It's there now, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, we can see that this is the message related to the meeting with Ganic, as attended by Gobilliard, Fraser, who was actually sending the report. And under item 2 on the next page reads: "General Gobilliard began the meeting and then he said that another incident had happened in a demilitarised zone and the exclusion zone of heavy weaponry involving 200 troops of the 4th Brigade, the members of the alleged Muslim league and the policemen." Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: This was one of a number of violations by the Bosnian government of this TEZ. I don't remember this specific one and I was not at this meeting, but it sounds like a correct account, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, Mr. Harland, take a look at the last item in this report compiled by Mr. Fraser, which reads -- the last page, paragraph 10: "Dr. Ganic appeared unaware of the troops in the TEZ/DMZ, but unconcerned. He was uncomfortable with the idea that the incident might be raised by Mr. Akashi and Defence Minister Perry. He was anxious that this not happen because of the impression that the Muslims were provoking the Serbians."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask that when the documents are put on the screen, they are highlighted so that we can see them in bigger print. It's difficult to read what is there now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this that I have read out enough or should I do it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that's fine. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence: "He did not deny the presence of the soldiers in the exclusion zone, demilitarised zone, but he tried to redirect, without success, the discussion to the attacks in the north around Bresa."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, I was not at this meeting, but it sounds like a very typical discussion with Dr. Ganic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to deal with one topic very swiftly. Do you know that General Dragomir Milosevic took the command over around the 10th of August or precisely on the 10th of August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I knew it was about that time because he appeared as the commander of the Romanija Corps in the discussions about the anti-sniping agreement, which I think was just after that time, yes, but I didn't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that several days earlier - I believe it was on the 4th of August, 1994; therefore, several days before he assumed the duty - the FRY introduced sanctions against the Army of Republika Srpska and that the sanctions were in force at the time General Milosevic took up his duties?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware of the sanctions and, in fact, we internationals were trying to encourage their imposition. But, you know, they were only partially successful of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, at one point you said - and I don't have time now to go and find exactly where this was - that the Serbs were evidently concerned about the borders being closed, the borders opposite the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That's correct. Dr. Karadzic raised it with us several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am about to broach quite a broad topic that deals with sniping. And it was mostly for that topic that I wanted to deal with your statement that you gave to the OTP investigators on the 17th of April, 1997, on the 13th of January, 9th of February, and the 10th of February, 1998, and which concerns sniping. I do not wish to go back to the agreement that was already discussed, because I don't want to analyse the matters concerning the agreement. The agreement was already tendered into evidence by the Prosecution. Nevertheless, I do have a couple of questions. In the statement, when discussing the anti-sniping agreement at page 11, the second paragraph, and the one immediately following it in the English version. In the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of the interpreters at page 10, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- the following is stated: "From the end of July until the 14th of August, we had a series of abortive meetings." These were your words. "They were mainly abortive, but nevertheless the agreement was signed." Therefore, for several months from the 14th of July, you were negotiating unsuccessfully. Dragomir Milosevic took up his duties on the 10th of August; and there -- and then on the 14th of August, he signed this anti-sniping agreement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the paragraph before that one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just to correct the record. That paragraph you just quoted from the witness statement, "from the end of July until 14th August." It's a little bit different. After the abortive meetings, "they were mainly abortive because of the lack of interest in an agreement by Tolimir and Indjic who were obstructing the negotiations." Just to complete the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi, this is precisely what I was referring to, the obstruction. There was obstruction of the agreement; however, Mr. Milosevic signed the agreement, in spite of all the previous obstruction. This is precisely what I wanted to hear, whether this was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the previous paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please state the answer for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in the position to confirm that, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask Mr. Harland to confirm his answer verbally and not just by nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I asked the witness whether he was in a position to confirm that. And what is your answer, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm in a position to confirm it, and I can also say that we were making no progress when we wanted to have an agreement to create a physical barrier that would stop snipers from being able to see the other side. And at the last meeting, we made what we felt was a -- a major concession, which is that we would not have the authority to actually hunt down violating snipers and -- in Article 2, and we would not actually have any construction of a physical barrier. And at that point, the Serbs agreed to sign; before that, they had not. So Mr. Tapuskovic's chronology is essentially correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in the previous paragraph you said, literally: "The background to this agreement is that the Blue Routes were closed in part due to the sniping by the Bosniaks of Serb civilians." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then at page 11, the last paragraph in the English version, you stated what you stated, in fact, today, that the agreement worked well for a period in the first couple of months when sniping was quite rare?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the agreement also said that the parties should publicly, or rather, that a public statement should be issued to the effect that the Serb side honoured this while the Muslims did not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No. I remember that we asked that both sides make public statements that -- that they were promoting the -- the agreement; and then, if I remember correctly, the famous incident in which two young Serb girls were killed in Grbavica happened before the agreement; and that then after the agreement -- and there had been a large number of sniper casualties on both sides; and that after the agreement - actually, if I remember correctly - the number of sniper incidents on both sides dropped away almost to zero for many weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the two young Serb girls. Was this in the month of August? Weren't you perhaps mistaken there? Did this not happen in the month of March during the violation of the agreement? Actually, they were killed during a truce that was supposed to last for four months?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I cannot now remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also said that whenever it was possible to monitor a sniping at Grbavica, the impression was that Bosnians were the ones who were sniping more extensively than the Serbs. That's at page 24, paragraph 5 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That was our impression from counting both sniper rounds and sniper victims in the Grbavica area and the adjacent areas controlled by the Bosnian government, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Tapuskovic. There's a very important point which you addressed, and I'm wondering if we couldn't get back to that. You mentioned the death of two young Serb girls. Is that right? Because we don't have the date of that incident. You are hesitating. And if we don't know, you've checked this with the witness and you wondered whether this was in March or in August. You must understand that this is a very important point. Is there any official UN document or any other document that could help you remember the day when these two young girls were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, we kept a full record. And it could be found in the daily situation reports of Sector Sarajevo, though I would just mention, Your Honour, that there were a large amount of sniper deaths on both sides, and this particular incident was one of very many. But it became famous because there was so much discussion around how -- whether or not one bullet had killed both of the girls. So in my -- it can be checked, but in my memory I cannot with absolute certainty distinguish the date of this incident from that of a large number of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Mindua, a lot of time has passed since, and it is quite possible that Mr. Harland cannot state this with any precision. But I'm sure in due time we will be able to clarify this matter, and I will not insist on the date, whether it happened in August of 1994 or in March of 1995. It isn't that important really. At any rate, he knows about the case when two young Serb girls aged 12 or 13 were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also said that you had some doubts about the command and control that the respective sides had over their snipers, and that the French were not certain whether the shots were fired -- that were fired on Bosniaks from a great distance actually originated from Serbs or Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tapuskovic please speak into his own microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the reference to the statement of the page that he just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you're being asked to speak into your own microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. It was often not possible from to a victim's wounds to tell where the firing point was located. That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I will be doing my best to try and refer as little as possible to the documents prior to the tenure of Mr. Milosevic. But I do have a document dated the 3rd of November, 1993, which was drafted by Mr. Harland and was then forwarded by Mr. Victor Andreev to Sergio De Mello. I would like to present Mr. Harland with only one paragraph thereof. R001449 is the number of the document. Could we look at page R0014152 -- or no, no, no, I'm sorry. That's the anti-sniping agreement. This is R0029446.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could Mr. Tapuskovic please speak slowly when citing numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've grown a bit tired with all the business with the papers now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, never mind that. The interpreter is asking you to speak more slowly when citing the numbers and the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've grown a bit weary of this, that's why, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's too early in the day for that, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. There we go. It's here. That's the English version. That's at page 3 of the English version, in the middle of the page. That's the fourth paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The text reads: "BH snipers have been firing on UN personnel around UNPROFOR's forward HQ. Two Bosnian snipers have been firing not only at UN personnel, but also at local pedestrians in the vicinity. BH Corps claims that these snipers are 'renegade supporters of Caco.'"

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that. And, in fact, I remember the incident and I, in fact, was present when those snipers were shooting around that area. And I spoke also with the anti-sniping teams from UNPROFOR that identified the exact sniping positions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain something else. You mentioned local pedestrians, does it mean that they were firing on Muslim citizens?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, you can't tell whether somebody is Muslim or Serb or Croat, but they were certainly firing on civilians who were inside -- in the Bosnian-controlled territory. Yes, that's correct. Also, I think, on Djure Djakovica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At page 6 of your statement you gave to investigators, paragraph 2, you talk about an assessment you made concerning snipers. I don't know if you found this bit.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "In this assessment I also indicated that in the area of the forward HQ of UNPROFOR, two Bosnian snipers were active who also fired on UN personnel." Is that more or less the same statement you made that we looked at just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yeah, it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this incident, I do recall that the French brought two of their own snipers to find -- find these two and kill them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and I met those two French snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you've met them. Can you tell us, did they liquidate them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: At the moment I talked to them, they had not. They had identified the firing point. Actually, they were a team. One of them seemed to hold some sort of telescopic sight, and the other one had a gun with a telescopic sight. And the one who was principally trying to identify the firing points had located actually more than one firing point, and they were able to point them out to me. And those firing points were certainly within Bosnian government-held territory, and then I was able to see for myself that sniper fire was opened from one of those positions and that it -- the sniper fire landed also in Bosnian government-held territory near the bottom of Djure Djakovica Street, causing a few civilian pedestrians to run quickly for hiding, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to finish this particular chapter, if I may. This is very important and is linked with what we've just been discussing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And how much longer will you be in your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do believe that I shall need some more time. I don't know how much was -- is envisaged within the six hours. I do believe that I should address the matters thoroughly, in view of the documents that I have. At first there were ten hours set aside, which were then reduced to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When is your next witness, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Witness Fortin, and he's available. He will be next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would half an hour more tomorrow be enough for you, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I'm sure this will not be enough. I do have several important topics that I haven't addressed yet and which are even more important than the ones I've done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The witness, as you know, has been scheduled for five or six hours, I might be mistaken. So we are still within that range, although you might have additional questions. And it's a first witness, and I can assure you that the next witnesses will be short and well within the time allocated. So while this first witness might be a little bit longer than anticipated, you know, the other ones might be a little bit shorter. So by the end of this week I'm sure we will be well within the schedule, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, one hour, would that enable you to complete your cross-examination? The witness was scheduled for five. The Prosecutor did overrun his time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Robinson, I will do my best to stay within the time. I'm not sure whether I will be able to, but I will try to cut down the issues I still have left this afternoon and to try and finish within the time given. But could I perhaps just finish this one sentence that we are dealing with right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have to adjourn immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I would like to hear whether the following is true, in the context of the meeting between General Rose and the BiH commander: "I do recall that we continued making comments about this over the following several months more than once. During the meeting with Mr. Ganic, General Rose complained about mortars mounted on trucks and sniper fire opened by Bosnians on their own people. Ganic's customary reply was to say that Rose was anti-Muslim." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Is what true, sorry? Is it true that he said that, or is it true that he was anti-Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is all of what I said true, that Rose, along those lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, do you wish to say something before the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just the source. Is it Mr. Harland's witness statement, is it Rose's book, is it a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're reading from the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the statement dated 17 February and then the other dates, at page 6, as I indicated a moment ago. And this is before Mr. Harland, this text, and is what I just read out true, correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That is correct. I made that statement and I knew those facts because I was in those meetings between General Rose and Dr. Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We must adjourn now, and we resume tomorrow at 2.15 here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of January, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
